modern: In my father I observed gentleness of temper, and unchangeable resolution in the things which he had decided after due deliberation; and no vanity about the things which men call honours; and a love of work, and perseverance; and a readiness to listen to those who had anything to propose for the common good; and unwavering firmness in giving to every man according to what he deserved; and a knowledge, gained from experience, of the occasions for vigorous action and for relaxation. And I observed that he had overcome all passion for boys; and he considered himself no more than any other citizen; and he released his friends from all obligation to dine with him or to attend him as a matter of course when he went out, and those who had failed to go with him, because of some urgent circumstance, always found him the same. I observed too his habit of careful inquiry in all matters for deliberation, and his persistence, and that he never stopped his investigation through being satisfied with the appearances which first present themselves; and that his disposition was to keep his friends, and not to be soon tired of them, nor yet to be extravagant in his affection; and to be content on all occasions, and cheerful; and to foresee things a long way off, and to provide for the smallest without display; and to check at once popular applause and all flattery; and to be always watchful over the things which were necessary for the administration of the empire, and to be a good manager of expenditure, and to endure patiently the blame which he got for such conduct; and he was neither superstitious with respect to the gods, nor did he court men by gifts or by trying to please them, or by flattering the people; but he showed moderation in all things, and firmness, and never any mean thoughts or actions, nor love of novelty. And the things which contribute in any way to the comfort of life, and of which fortune gives an abundant supply, he used without arrogance and without apology; so that when he had them, he enjoyed them without affectation, and when he did not have them, he did not miss them. No one could ever say of him that he was either a sophist or a flippant, home-bred slave or a pedant; but everyone acknowledged him to be a man mature, complete, above flattery, able to manage his own and other men’s affairs. Besides this, he honoured those who were true philosophers, and he did not reproach those who pretended to be philosophers, nor yet was he easily led by them. He was also easy in conversation, and he made himself pleasant without any offensive affectation. He took reasonable care of his body’s health, not as one who was greatly attached to life, nor out of concern for his personal appearance, nor yet in a careless way, but so that, through his own attention, he very seldom needed the art of the physician, or medicine, or external applications. He was most ready to give, without envy, to those who had any particular ability, such as eloquence or knowledge of the law or of morals, or of anything else; and he gave them his help, so that each might enjoy a reputation according to his merits; and he always acted in keeping with the institutions of his country, without showing any affectation of doing so. Further, he was not fond of change, nor unsteady, but he loved to stay in the same places, and to occupy himself with the same things; and after his attacks of headache he came at once, fresh and vigorous, to his usual occupations. His secrets were not many, but very few and very rare, and these only about public matters; and he showed prudence and economy in putting on public spectacles, in the construction of public buildings, in his gifts to the people, and in such things, for he was a man who looked to what ought to be done, not to the reputation which a man gets by his acts. He did not bathe at unusual hours; he was not fond of building houses, nor particular about what he ate, nor about the texture and colour of his clothes, nor about the beauty of his slaves. His clothes came from Lorium, his villa on the coast, and from Lanuvium generally. We know how he behaved to the toll-collector at Tusculum who asked his pardon; and all his behaviour was like that. There was nothing in him harsh, nor unforgiving, nor violent, nor, as one might say, anything carried to the point of sweating; but he examined all things one by one, as if he had plenty of time, and without confusion, in an orderly way, vigorously and consistently. And what is recorded of Socrates might be applied to him: that he was able both to abstain from, and to enjoy, those things which many are too weak to abstain from, and cannot enjoy without excess. But to be strong enough both to bear the one and to be sober in the other is the mark of a man who has a perfect and invincible soul, such as he showed in the illness of Maximus.
